corrected_answer:
Assumption frame: single node, 8x NVIDIA A30 24 GB (HBM2, ~933 GB/s theoretical peak, PCIe Gen4 x16 host links, no NVLink bridge assumed), dense ~9B decoder in bf16 (~18 GB weights), paged KV cache, vLLM-class iteration-level scheduler. All numbers are ESTIMATES from a roofline/queueing model unless explicitly labelled MEASURED.

Contrast: continuous batching vs. static (request-level) batching, variant 4.

Concrete mechanism. A static batcher forms a batch of N requests, runs the whole generation loop to completion for that batch, then forms the next one. Because sequences finish at different lengths, the batch is padded to the longest member and every finished slot keeps executing padded decode steps until the slowest sequence terminates. Continuous batching instead re-evaluates the running set at every iteration boundary: after each decode step the scheduler retires any sequence that emitted EOS or hit max_tokens, frees its KV blocks back to the paged allocator, and admits waiting requests into the freed slots before the next forward pass. The unit of scheduling changes from "one request" to "one token step".

Why it wins. Useful-token efficiency under static batching is approximately mean(L)/max(L) over the batch's output lengths. For a realistic chat mix with a heavy tail (mean ~120 tokens, p99 ~2000), that ratio is often 0.1-0.3, so 70-90% of decode slot-steps are wasted on padding. Continuous batching drives that ratio toward 1.0 minus scheduler overhead, so throughput gain is roughly max(L)/mean(L) in the length-dispersion-limited regime. It is NOT a gain when output lengths are uniform.

Boundary condition. The advantage collapses when output length dispersion is near zero. If every request emits exactly the same number of tokens (fixed-length classification, forced-decoding scoring, single-token logprob queries), a static batch has no padding waste and continuous batching adds only overhead: per-iteration scheduling, block-table rebuild, and CUDA-graph invalidation whenever the running-set shape changes. In that regime static batching with a large fixed batch can be measurably faster.

Second boundary condition: continuous batching cannot help if the KV cache, not the slot count, is the binding constraint. Per-token KV bytes = 2 (K and V) * n_layers * n_kv_heads * head_dim * dtype_bytes. Once KV utilisation is pinned near the high-water mark, freeing a finished sequence's blocks only lets in a new request if the new request's projected KV footprint fits; otherwise the scheduler idles slots it nominally has.

Falsifiable hypotheses.
H1: If dispersion drives the gap, then throughput gain over static batching correlates with the batch's max_len/mean_len ratio; forcing all requests to identical output length should shrink the gap to <10%.
H2: If the bottleneck is KV capacity rather than scheduling, raising gpu_memory_utilization (and thus KV blocks) should raise throughput while the running-sequence count rises; if running count does not rise, H2 is false.

Evidence required before acting. (a) Distribution of output lengths (mean, p50, p99) from server logs, not a synthetic benchmark. (b) Server counters: running vs waiting sequences, KV utilisation %, preemption/recompute counter, per-iteration step time. (c) A paired A/B on the same traffic replay, not on different days.

Rollback gate. Ship the scheduler change only if p99 TTFT does not regress more than 10% and the preemption counter stays at zero at target QPS for a full peak window; otherwise revert to the prior scheduling config, since continuous batching's admission aggressiveness can trade tail latency for throughput.

Operational caution. Do not enable aggressive admission and raise gpu_memory_utilization in the same change; you will not be able to attribute a regression.

Contrast: continuous batching vs. a naive non-continuous implementation, variant 5.

Concrete mechanism. The naive path couples request lifetime to batch lifetime: batch admission happens once, the forward loop runs until the longest sequence terminates, and KV memory is provisioned per slot as a contiguous, worst-case reservation of max_seq_len. Continuous batching decouples both dimensions. (1) Scheduling: the running set is recomputed at each iteration boundary, so a request can join at step k and leave at step k+j independently of its neighbours. (2) Memory: with paged KV, a sequence holds a block table of fixed-size pages (commonly 16 tokens/page) allocated on demand, so it consumes KV proportional to tokens actually generated rather than to max_seq_len.

Quantified consequence of the memory half. Contiguous worst-case reservation with max_seq_len = 8192 but mean realised length ~600 tokens wastes ~93% of reserved KV. Paged allocation reduces internal fragmentation to at most one partially filled page per sequence, i.e. <16 tokens of waste, so concurrency at fixed KV budget rises by roughly max_seq_len/mean_len. That is usually the larger of the two effects, and it is easy to misattribute to the scheduler.

Boundary condition. The naive implementation is not strictly worse when requests are homogeneous AND short-lived AND the deployment is latency-floor-bound rather than throughput-bound. Concretely, at low QPS where the running set never exceeds one or two sequences, decode time is (weights + KV)/BW_eff and is dominated by the ~18 GB weight read; adding batching of either flavour changes almost nothing, while continuous batching's per-iteration Python-side scheduling can add measurable fixed overhead per step. Below that crossover, the naive path can be the faster one.

Falsifiable hypotheses.
H1: If the win is memory-driven, replacing contiguous KV with paged KV while keeping static request-level batching should recover most of the concurrency gain. If it does not, the win is scheduler-driven.
H2: If per-iteration scheduling overhead is material, step time at running=1 should exceed the roofline estimate (~18 GB / (0.7*933 GB/s) ~= 28 ms) by a visible constant; if measured step time matches roofline within noise, overhead is not the issue.

Evidence required. MEASURED per-step time at running=1, 4, 16; KV utilisation and block-table size; preemption counter; and a memory-fragmentation report. Roofline arithmetic must be recomputed with the actual n_kv_heads/head_dim of the served checkpoint, not assumed.

Rollback gate. Revert if preemption/recompute events become non-zero at steady state, or if p99 ITL regresses beyond the SLO, whichever comes first. Preemption thrash is the specific failure mode that turns a throughput win into a tail-latency disaster.

Safety note. Never validate this change by comparing against a benchmark whose prompts share the tuning traffic; that measures memoisation of the workload shape, not scheduler quality.

corrected_answer:
Assumption frame: single node, 8x NVIDIA A30 24 GB (HBM2, ~933 GB/s theoretical peak, PCIe Gen4 x16 host links, no NVLink bridge assumed), dense ~9B decoder in bf16 (~18 GB weights), paged KV cache, vLLM-class iteration-level scheduler. All numbers are ESTIMATES from a roofline/queueing model unless explicitly labelled MEASURED.

Two failure modes / trade-offs of continuous batching, variant 1.

Failure mode 1: preemption and recompute thrash under KV pressure.
Mechanism. The scheduler admits requests based on currently free KV blocks, but a sequence's future KV growth is unknown at admission time. If admitted sequences all keep generating, the allocator runs out of blocks mid-flight, and the engine must preempt: either swap a victim's KV to host memory over PCIe or drop it and recompute its prefix later. Recompute costs the full prefill of the victim's context again; swap costs KV_bytes / PCIe_bw each way (Gen4 x16 gives ~25 GB/s realised, so a 2 GB KV state is ~80 ms out plus ~80 ms back, per victim). Under sustained overload, victims are re-admitted and preempted again, and goodput collapses while GPU utilisation still looks high.
Boundary condition. This only occurs once KV utilisation crosses the admission high-water mark; below it, preemption count is identically zero and the failure mode cannot be present. That makes it directly falsifiable: if the preemption counter is 0 during the incident window, this is not your bug.

Failure mode 2: throughput/tail-latency trade-off from head-of-line interference.
Mechanism. Every co-running sequence adds its KV read to each decode step, so per-step time grows roughly as (W + sum_i KV_i)/BW_eff. Admitting more sequences raises aggregate token throughput but raises inter-token latency for every sequence already running, including short interactive ones. A single long-context request with a multi-hundred-MB KV state can inflate ITL for all its neighbours. Additionally, prefill of a newly admitted long prompt is compute-heavy and, if not chunked, occupies a step that decoding sequences must wait on, producing an ITL spike.
Boundary condition. The interference is bounded by the KV budget: it saturates once the running set is capped by memory rather than by admission policy, and it is negligible when sum_i KV_i is small relative to the 18 GB weight read, i.e. at low concurrency or short contexts.

Falsifiable hypotheses.
H1: If tail ITL spikes coincide with newly admitted long prompts, enabling chunked prefill should cut p99 ITL without changing mean throughput. If p99 is unchanged, H1 is false.
H2: If the incident is preemption thrash, lowering max_num_seqs should raise goodput; if goodput falls, the system was not preemption-limited.

Evidence required. Time-aligned series of: preemption/swap counter, KV utilisation, running/waiting counts, p50/p99 ITL, and prompt-length distribution of admissions in the same window. Correlation without the counter series is not evidence.

Rollback gate. Any admission-policy change ships only behind a flag with a single-command revert, and only if, over a full peak window, preemption stays zero and p99 ITL stays within SLO. Roll back immediately on the first sustained non-zero preemption rate.

Provisional caveat: these are mechanism-level expectations; none is confirmed for this deployment without the MEASURED counters above.

Two failure modes / trade-offs of continuous batching, variant 2.

Failure mode 1: CUDA-graph and kernel-shape instability.
Mechanism. Continuous batching changes the running-set size at essentially every iteration. Engines that capture CUDA graphs to amortise launch overhead must capture per batch-shape and fall back to eager execution on an uncaptured shape. With a fluctuating running set, the shape distribution is wide, so either graph capture memory grows (one replay buffer per bucketed shape) or the hit rate drops and per-step launch overhead reappears. On a decode step whose useful work is ~20-30 ms, tens of kernel launches at a few microseconds each are tolerable, but an eager fallback on a deep model with hundreds of launches per layer is not.
Boundary condition. Only material when per-step compute is small relative to launch overhead, i.e. small models or small running sets. For a ~9B model at running>=8 the step is memory-bound and launch overhead is a low-single-digit percentage. Falsifiable: if eager vs graph-captured step time differs by <2% at your operating concurrency, this is not your bottleneck.

Failure mode 2: fairness and starvation under a throughput-greedy admission policy.
Mechanism. A scheduler that maximises tokens/second prefers keeping the running set full of cheap, short-KV sequences and can repeatedly defer or preempt long-context requests, whose re-admission requires a large contiguous-ish block allocation. The result is unbounded waiting time for the requests that already cost the most, i.e. a starvation pattern that shows up as a bimodal TTFT distribution rather than a shifted mean. Aggregate throughput dashboards look healthy throughout.
Boundary condition. Bounded by any explicit aging/priority term in the scheduler; if the policy promotes by waiting time, starvation is capped at the aging horizon. It also cannot occur when offered load is below the KV-capacity knee, since nothing is deferred.

Falsifiable hypotheses.
H1: If starvation is present, TTFT conditioned on prompt length will be bimodal and the upper mode will correlate with waiting-queue depth; a length-blind slowdown falsifies H1.
H2: If graph instability matters, pinning max_num_seqs to a single value (removing shape churn) should reduce mean step time; no change falsifies H2.

Evidence required. Per-request TTFT joined to prompt length and admission timestamp; queue-depth series; graph-capture hit-rate counters or an eager-mode A/B at fixed concurrency; step-time histogram, not just the mean.

Rollback gate. Do not deploy a fairness fix that raises p99 TTFT for any length bucket. Gate on: no length bucket regresses >10% at p99, preemption stays zero, and aggregate throughput loss is <5%. Revert on breach of any one.

Operational safety. Changing max_num_seqs on a live server usually requires a restart; drain the node behind the load balancer first rather than restarting under traffic, otherwise in-flight requests are lost and the experiment is confounded by retries.

These are provisional mechanism-level claims, not validated findings for this cluster.

All numbers are ESTIMATES from a roofline/queueing model unless explicitly labelled MEASURED.

Two failure modes / trade-offs of continuous batching, variant 3.

Failure mode 1: prefill/decode interference (the "one big prompt stalls everyone" pattern).
Mechanism. Prefill is compute-bound: it processes P prompt tokens in parallel, costing roughly 2*N_params*P FLOPs (~18 GFLOP per token for a 9B model at forward-only 2*params). Decode is memory-bound. When an iteration-level scheduler admits a long prompt without chunking, that single iteration must run the whole prefill before any co-running sequence gets its next token. A 4096-token prompt at ~18 GFLOP/token is ~74 TFLOP; on an A30 at a realistic bf16 efficiency the prefill step is on the order of hundreds of milliseconds, i.e. 10x-30x a normal decode step. Every co-running sequence sees that as one enormous inter-token gap.
Boundary condition. Bounded above by the largest admitted prompt and eliminated by chunked prefill, which caps tokens-per-prefill-slice; with a slice budget of, say, 512 tokens, worst-case added ITL is one slice's compute rather than a whole prompt's. The failure mode cannot appear in a decode-only workload (all prompts already cached).

Failure mode 2: throughput accounting that hides goodput loss.
Mechanism. Continuous batching maximises tokens processed, but preempted-and-recomputed prefix tokens are counted as processed work. A server can report rising tokens/second while user-visible completed-requests/second falls, because a growing fraction of the tokens are recomputation of previously computed prefixes. This is the specific reason throughput dashboards are not a safety signal for scheduler changes.
Boundary condition. Only possible when preemption is non-zero; with zero preemptions, processed tokens equal useful tokens up to speculative-decoding rejects.

Falsifiable hypotheses.
H1: If interference is prefill-driven, ITL spikes will be time-aligned with admissions of prompts above some length threshold; enabling chunked prefill should cut p99 ITL by roughly the ratio of max prompt length to slice size. No alignment falsifies H1.
H2: If goodput is being lost to recompute, completed-requests/second will diverge downward from tokens/second as load rises; parallel movement falsifies H2.

Evidence required. (a) Per-iteration trace with a prefill/decode tag and token counts. (b) Preemption and recomputed-token counters. (c) Completed-requests/second alongside tokens/second, plotted against offered load. (d) Prompt-length distribution. Nsight Systems traces only after the counter-level evidence points at a specific step type; profiling first is expensive and usually misdirected.

Rollback gate. Enable chunked prefill behind a flag; keep it only if p99 ITL improves and p99 TTFT regresses by less than 10% (chunking does trade some TTFT for ITL smoothness). Revert on any increase in preemption count or in completed-request error rate.

Provisional: mechanism-level reasoning with stated assumptions; not a MEASURED result for this deployment.

Two failure modes / trade-offs of continuous batching, variant 4.

Failure mode 1: admission based on current rather than projected KV footprint.
Mechanism. The scheduler admits a request if free KV blocks cover its prompt, but a sequence's total KV demand is prompt + generated tokens, and the generated count is unknown a priori. With paged KV, blocks are appended lazily, so an over-admitted running set discovers the shortfall only after several decode steps, at which point the only remedies are preemption (swap or recompute) or refusing to grow, which stalls a sequence mid-generation. The observable signature is a sawtooth in KV utilisation plus a nonzero preemption counter at steady offered load.
Boundary condition. Cannot occur if max_tokens is small and uniformly enforced such that worst-case KV of the full running set fits the budget: worst_case = sum_i (P_i + max_tokens_i) * kv_bytes_per_token <= KV_budget. Under that admission invariant the failure mode is structurally impossible, at the cost of lower average concurrency.

Failure mode 2: retry amplification interacting with iteration-level admission.
Mechanism. When tail latency rises, clients time out and retry. Continuous batching happily admits the retries alongside the still-running originals, so each timeout multiplies offered KV demand instead of shedding it. This is a positive feedback loop: latency up -> retries up -> KV pressure up -> preemption up -> latency up. Static batching's coarse admission accidentally damps this; iteration-level admission does not.
Boundary condition. Requires client-side retry with a timeout shorter than the degraded p99. If clients do not retry, or if the server cancels the original on client disconnect, the loop cannot close.

Falsifiable hypotheses.
H1: If retry amplification is active, admitted-requests/second will exceed unique-requests/second during the incident; equality falsifies H1.
H2: If over-admission is the cause, enforcing the worst-case admission invariant above should drive preemption to zero at the cost of lower running-set size. If preemption persists at zero over-admission, some other component (e.g. a memory leak in the block allocator) is responsible.

Evidence required. Unique vs admitted request counts (requires a client-supplied idempotency/request ID); KV utilisation time series with the admission high-water mark drawn on it; preemption counter; client timeout configuration; and confirmation that the server cancels work on disconnect.

Rollback gate and safety. Mitigations are ordered least-destructive first: (1) enable disconnect cancellation, (2) add server-side admission backpressure returning 429 with Retry-After rather than queueing unboundedly, (3) only then tune max_num_seqs. Each step behind a flag, each validated over a full peak window, revert on any increase in 5xx or in completed-request error rate. Do not restart the engine under live traffic to apply a config change; drain the replica first.

Provisional mechanism analysis, not a validated incident finding; every quantitative claim needs the MEASURED counters listed above.

Assumption frame: single node, 8x NVIDIA A30 24 GB (HBM2, ~933 GB/s theoretical peak, PCIe Gen4 x16 host links, no NVLink bridge assumed), dense ~9B decoder in bf16 (~18 GB weights), paged KV cache, vLLM-class iteration-level scheduler. Two failure modes / trade-offs of continuous batching, variant 5.

Failure mode 1: interaction with tensor parallelism turns a scheduling change into a collective-communication problem.
Mechanism. Under TP=k the running set is replicated across k ranks and every decode step contains 2 all-reduces per transformer layer (after attention output projection and after the MLP). Those collectives are synchronous: the step advances at the speed of the slowest rank. Continuous batching's per-iteration re-planning must therefore be identical on all ranks; any divergence (e.g. a rank computing a different running-set order) deadlocks or corrupts the collective. Even when correct, per-step all-reduce latency is a fixed additive cost that does not shrink with batch size, so raising concurrency improves throughput but never reduces the per-step floor. Without NVLink, those all-reduces traverse PCIe and the floor is materially higher; NCCL will fall back to PCIe/SHM paths, and P2P availability should be confirmed rather than assumed.
Boundary condition. Negligible when TP=1. Bounded below by the all-reduce latency of the smallest message: at TP=8 on PCIe, small-message ring all-reduce latency is dominated by hop count, so the floor scales with the number of ranks, not with payload.

Failure mode 2: scheduler-induced nondeterminism in outputs.
Mechanism. Which sequences are co-batched changes the GEMM shapes and hence the reduction order in floating-point accumulation. bf16 accumulation is not associative, so identical prompts with identical seeds can produce different logits at the last decimal places and, near a sampling boundary, different tokens. Continuous batching makes co-batching traffic-dependent, so reproducibility becomes a function of concurrent load.
Boundary condition. Only observable when the argmax margin is smaller than the accumulated numerical error; greedy decoding with a well-separated top token is stable. It is therefore a correctness concern for eval harnesses and regression tests, not usually for user traffic.

Falsifiable hypotheses.
H1: If the per-step floor is collective-bound, step time at running=1 will scale with TP degree rather than staying flat; flat scaling falsifies H1 and points back at HBM bandwidth.
H2: If nondeterminism is co-batching-driven, replaying the same eval set at concurrency=1 should be bit-reproducible while concurrency=32 is not.

Evidence required. NCCL bandwidth/latency baseline from nccl-tests at the relevant message sizes; per-step timing at TP=1,2,4,8 at fixed concurrency; nvidia-smi topo -m to confirm the actual link topology instead of assuming it; and a repeated-run diff of eval outputs at two concurrency levels.

Rollback gate. Never change TP degree and scheduler policy together. Gate any TP change on nccl-tests bus bandwidth meeting the expected fraction of link capacity and on a bit-level eval reproducibility check at concurrency=1; revert on failure of either.

source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer:
Assumption frame: single node, 8x NVIDIA A30 24 GB (HBM2, ~933 GB/s theoretical peak, PCIe Gen4 x16 host links, no NVLink bridge assumed), dense ~9B decoder in bf16 (~18 GB weights), paged KV cache, vLLM-class iteration-level scheduler. All numbers are ESTIMATES from a roofline/queueing model unless explicitly labelled MEASURED.

How continuous batching interacts with latency, throughput, and memory, variant 1.

Concrete mechanism. The scheduler recomputes the running set at every iteration boundary; per decode step the GPU reads the full weight set once plus the KV state of every running sequence. Step time ~= (W + sum_i KV_i) / BW_eff, with W ~= 18 GB and BW_eff ~= 0.65-0.75 * 933 GB/s on A30. The weight term is amortised across all co-running sequences; the KV term is not.

Throughput. Tokens/second ~= R / step_time where R is the running-set size. Because W dominates at small R, throughput rises nearly linearly with R at first, then flattens once sum_i KV_i approaches W. That crossover is the single most useful quantity in capacity planning: below it you are paying for weight reads, above it you are paying for KV reads and adding concurrency buys little. With ~9B-class KV geometry and multi-thousand-token contexts, the crossover typically lands at a few tens of concurrent sequences, but the exact value must be MEASURED, not assumed, because it depends on n_kv_heads and head_dim of the actual checkpoint.

Latency. Per-sequence inter-token latency equals the step time, so every additional co-running sequence slows every other one. Continuous batching therefore converts a latency budget into a concurrency cap: given an ITL SLO, the maximum admissible sum_i KV_i is SLO * BW_eff - W. Requests with long contexts consume that budget disproportionately. TTFT is governed separately by queueing plus prefill compute; chunked prefill trades a small TTFT increase for much smaller ITL spikes.

Memory. Paged KV makes the memory footprint proportional to tokens actually materialised, capping internal fragmentation at under one page (commonly 16 tokens) per sequence, versus a contiguous max_seq_len reservation that can waste over 90% at typical realised lengths. Total budget = HBM - weights - activations - fragmentation headroom; on 24 GB A30 with 18 GB of bf16 weights on a single card there is almost nothing left, which is why a 9B bf16 model realistically needs TP>=2 to leave a usable KV budget. That is a deployment constraint, not a statement about model capability.

Boundary condition. The linear-throughput regime ends exactly where sum_i KV_i ~= W; past it, added concurrency raises tail latency roughly proportionally while adding little aggregate throughput, and it increases preemption risk.

Falsifiable hypotheses.
H1: Throughput vs running-set size will be concave with a knee at sum_i KV_i ~= W. A straight line to the memory limit falsifies the roofline model and suggests a scheduler-side bottleneck instead.
H2: If ITL is bandwidth-bound, measured step time will track (W + sum KV)/BW_eff within ~15%; a large constant offset indicates launch overhead or collective latency instead.

Evidence required. source_user: Explain how continuous batching interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 2: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer:
Assumption frame: single node, 8x NVIDIA A30 24 GB (HBM2, ~933 GB/s theoretical peak, PCIe Gen4 x16 host links, no NVLink bridge assumed), dense ~9B decoder in bf16 (~18 GB weights), paged KV cache, vLLM-class iteration-level scheduler. All numbers are ESTIMATES from a roofline/queueing model unless explicitly labelled MEASURED.

How continuous batching interacts with latency, throughput, and memory, variant 2.

Mechanism, stated as a budget. Continuous batching converts three separate resources into one shared, per-iteration allocation problem:
- Bandwidth budget per step: bytes_read = W + sum_i KV_i, so step_time = bytes_read / BW_eff.
- Memory budget: KV_budget = HBM_per_gpu * gpu_memory_utilization - weights_shard - activation_peak.
- Latency budget: ITL_SLO >= step_time, which caps sum_i KV_i at ITL_SLO * BW_eff - W.
The scheduler's admission decision at each iteration boundary is feasible only if all three hold simultaneously. Most production incidents are a case of satisfying the memory budget while silently violating the latency budget, because the memory limit is enforced by the allocator and the latency limit is not enforced by anything.

Throughput consequence. Aggregate tokens/second = R/step_time. Substituting the bandwidth budget gives R * BW_eff / (W + sum KV). While sum KV << W this is approximately R * BW_eff / W, i.e. linear in R; the marginal value of the (R+1)-th sequence falls monotonically as KV accumulates. The practical implication: tune max_num_seqs to the latency budget, then use the memory budget only as a hard safety ceiling.

Memory consequence and a specific trap. Raising gpu_memory_utilization enlarges KV_budget and therefore lets the scheduler admit more sequences, which raises sum KV, which raises step time. Operators frequently raise this knob to fix preemption and are surprised when p99 ITL degrades. The two knobs are coupled through admission; they must be changed one at a time.

Boundary condition. If the deployment is TP-sharded, W in every formula is the per-GPU weight shard, not the whole model, and a per-step collective latency term must be added: step_time = (W_shard + sum KV_shard)/BW_eff + c_allreduce(TP, link). At TP=8 over PCIe without NVLink, c_allreduce can dominate at low concurrency, and none of the bandwidth reasoning above applies until that term is measured.

Falsifiable hypotheses.
H1: If admission is latency-violating rather than memory-violating, p99 ITL will exceed SLO while KV utilisation stays below the high-water mark and preemption stays zero. Non-zero preemption falsifies H1 and redirects to capacity.
H2: If c_allreduce dominates, step time at running=1 will be materially above W_shard/BW_eff and will grow with TP degree.

Evidence required. Per-step time and KV utilisation sampled together at 1 Hz or faster; nccl-tests all-reduce latency at the model's actual message sizes; nvidia-smi topo -m; the checkpoint config for exact kv_bytes_per_token; and an offered-load sweep with preemption held at zero.

Rollback gate. One knob per deployment. Hold each change for a full peak window. Revert immediately if p99 ITL breaches SLO, if preemption becomes non-zero, or if completed-requests/second falls while tokens/second rises (the goodput-divergence signature).

Provisional analysis under stated assumptions; every constant here is an estimate pending MEASURED data from this cluster.

source_user: Explain how continuous batching interacts with latency, throughput, or memory. Case variant 3: include one concrete mechanism and one boundary condition.
source_assistant: Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries so completed sequences do not hold a static batch slot.
corrected_answer:
Assumption frame: single node, 8x NVIDIA A30 24 GB (HBM2, ~933 GB/s theoretical peak, PCIe Gen4 x16 host links, no NVLink bridge assumed), dense ~9B decoder in bf16 (~18 GB weights), paged KV cache, vLLM-class iteration-level scheduler. All numbers are ESTIMATES from a roofline/queueing model unless explicitly labelled MEASURED.

How continuous batching interacts with latency, throughput, and memory, variant 3.

Mechanism, from the scheduler's point of view. At each iteration boundary the engine (1) retires finished sequences and frees their KV pages, (2) decides how many waiting requests to admit and whether to run a prefill slice or a decode step, (3) rebuilds the block tables and launches the forward pass. Steps (1) and (2) are what make batching "continuous"; step (3) is where latency, throughput and memory become coupled, because the shape of the launched kernel is determined by the admission decision.

Latency decomposition. TTFT = queue_wait + prefill_time(+ chunking overhead). ITL = step_time = (W + sum_i KV_i)/BW_eff (+ collective latency under TP). Continuous batching mainly improves queue_wait, because a request no longer waits for an entire batch to drain; it mainly worsens ITL, because it keeps the running set fuller. Any evaluation that reports only end-to-end latency will average these two opposing effects and can show "no change" while both p99 TTFT and p99 ITL moved substantially in opposite directions. Report TTFT and ITL separately, always.

Throughput. Useful-token efficiency rises from mean(L)/max(L) toward 1, so the expected gain over static batching scales with output-length dispersion. In a heavy-tailed chat mix that is often a 3x-10x effect; in a fixed-length scoring workload it is ~1x. Predict the gain from the measured length distribution before running the A/B, and treat a large discrepancy between predicted and measured gain as a signal that something else (KV capacity, collective latency, tokenizer/detokenizer CPU work) is the real bottleneck.

Memory. Paged KV plus iteration-level retirement means the footprint tracks live tokens, so peak KV is set by the concurrent live token count, not by max_seq_len * max_num_seqs. Capacity planning should therefore be done in units of concurrent live tokens: max_live_tokens = KV_budget / kv_bytes_per_token, and max_num_seqs is a derived quantity, not a primary one.

Boundary condition. All of this assumes prefix caching is either off or accounted for. With prefix/radix caching, shared prompt prefixes make sum_i KV_i sublinear in R, shifting the throughput knee substantially to the right. Cache hit rate is workload-dependent, so a benchmark with a shared system prompt will overstate production capacity; that is a contamination risk in benchmarking, not a capability gain.

Falsifiable hypotheses.
H1: If prefix caching is inflating results, disabling it should reduce measured max concurrency roughly in proportion to the shared-prefix fraction. No change falsifies H1.
H2: If CPU-side detokenisation is the bottleneck, GPU memory-controller utilisation will sit well below saturation while step time is flat and a CPU core is pinned. Saturated memory controllers falsify H2.

Evidence required. Separate TTFT and ITL percentiles; measured output-length distribution; kv_bytes_per_token from the served config; prefix-cache hit-rate counter; concurrent-live-token series; and CPU utilisation per server process alongside GPU counters.

Rollback gate. Publish capacity numbers only from a run with prefix caching configured as production has it, preemption at zero, and both TTFT and ITL percentiles inside SLO. Revert any tuning change that improves one percentile while breaching the other.

Provisional, assumption-bound, and explicitly not expert gold; these are mechanisms and tests, not validated measurements for this deployment.
risks: Source answer conflates TTFT and ITL, which move in opposite directions under continuous batching
Prefix caching can inflate benchmark capacity numbers (benchmark contamination risk)
Non-GPU bottlenecks (detokenisation) can be misdiagnosed as batching problems
evidence_required: Separate TTFT and ITL percentile series
Measured output-length distribution and prefix-cache hit rate
Concurrent-live-token series plus per-process CPU utilisation alongside GPU counters
